lede: Real readings go missing in more than one way: an empty value, a number that isn't a number, or a code like -9999 that only means "nothing here". Each needs a different test, and getting it wrong quietly corrupts every average and filter downstream.
objectives: Find missing values with `isNull` and `isNotNull`, and see why `== None` finds nothing
Tell NaN from NULL, find it with `isnan`, and know how it compares
Turn a sentinel code like -9999 into a real missing value with `na.replace`
Drop or fill missing values with `dropna`, `fillna` and `coalesce`

blocks.md:
The `observations` table above has one weather reading per row. It's loaded as a DataFrame called `observations`, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`. Three readings are broken in three different ways: one has no temperature, one rain gauge reported a fault, and one station sent its code for "no value" instead of a pressure.

An empty value is `NULL`. You can't find it with `==`: a comparison with `NULL` is never true (lesson 10), not even `== None`. Use `F.col("x").isNull()` or `isNotNull()`.

blocks.title: Find the empty temperature
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

print(observations.filter(F.col("temperature_c") == None).count(), "rows with == None")

observations.filter(F.col("temperature_c").isNull()).select("observation_id", "station_id", "temperature_c").show()
blocks.note: `== None` compares with `NULL`, which is never true, so it finds nothing and raises no error. `isNull()` finds the one reading.

blocks.md:
**NaN** ("not a number") is different. It's a real `double` value, the result of a calculation that failed, and here it marks a rain-gauge fault. `isNull()` is false for NaN; `F.isnan(col)` finds it.

NaN also compares in its own way in Spark: NaN equals NaN, and it's **bigger than every other number**. So `precipitation_mm > 0` is true for a fault, and a filter for "rain fell" would keep it unless you leave NaN out.

blocks.title: NaN is not NULL
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

observations.select(
    "observation_id",
    "precipitation_mm",
    F.col("precipitation_mm").isNull().alias("is_null"),
    F.isnan("precipitation_mm").alias("is_nan"),
    (F.col("precipitation_mm") > 0).alias("more_than_0"),
).show()
blocks.note: OBS-000006 is NaN: not null, but `isnan` is true, and so is `> 0`. Only the last two readings really had rain.

blocks.md: The third kind is a **sentinel**: an ordinary number that a system uses to mean "missing", here -9999. Spark can't know that, so it would happily average it. Turn it into a real `NULL` first. `df.na.replace(-9999, None, subset=[...])` does that in the columns you list and leaves the rest alone; `F.when` from lesson 17 works too.

blocks.title: Turn -9999 into NULL
blocks.code:
readings = ["temperature_c", "humidity_pct", "wind_speed_kph", "pressure_hpa"]
cleaned = observations.na.replace(-9999, None, subset=readings)

observations.select("observation_id", "pressure_hpa").show(3)
cleaned.select("observation_id", "pressure_hpa").show(3)
blocks.note: OBS-000002's pressure of -9999.0 is `NULL` afterwards. Every other value, and every other column, is unchanged.

blocks.md:
Once missing values are real `NULL`s, you can drop or fill them.

- `df.dropna()` drops a row if any column is missing. `subset=[...]` checks only some columns, `how="all"` drops a row only when all of them are missing, and `thresh=n` keeps rows with at least `n` values present. For number columns, NaN counts as missing too.
- `df.fillna(value)` puts `value` in place of missing values, in the columns of a matching type; a dict like `{"temperature_c": 0.0}` fills column by column. Number columns get their NaNs filled as well.
- `F.coalesce(a, b, ...)` takes the first value that isn't `NULL`, row by row.

blocks.title: Drop rows with missing values
blocks.code:
readings = ["temperature_c", "humidity_pct", "precipitation_mm", "wind_speed_kph", "pressure_hpa"]
cleaned = observations.na.replace(-9999, None, subset=readings)

print(cleaned.count(), "readings")
print(cleaned.dropna(subset=readings).count(), "with all five measurements")
print(cleaned.dropna(subset=["temperature_c"]).count(), "with a temperature")
print(cleaned.dropna(thresh=4, subset=readings).count(), "with at least four of the five")
blocks.note: Three readings are each missing one measurement, so nine have all five. The NaN reading counts as missing. Every reading still has at least four.

blocks.title: Fill missing values
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

small = observations.select("observation_id", "temperature_c", "precipitation_mm")

small.fillna({"precipitation_mm": 0.0}).select("observation_id", "precipitation_mm").show(7)

small.select(
    "observation_id",
    "temperature_c",
    F.coalesce(F.col("temperature_c"), F.lit(-99.0)).alias("temperature_or_marker"),
).show(12)
blocks.note: `fillna` turned the NaN fault into 0.0, which says it was dry: only fill when the value you put in is true. `coalesce` keeps each temperature and uses -99.0 only for the empty one; `F.lit(-99.0)` is a column with that same value on every row.

concept.prompt: How many rows does `observations.filter(F.col("temperature_c") == None)` keep when one reading has no temperature?
concept.why: A comparison with `NULL` is never true, so nothing passes. Use `isNull()` to find empty values.

concept.prompt: `precipitation_mm` is NaN on a row. Which of these is true for that row?
concept.why: NaN is a value, not `NULL`, so `isNull()` is false. Spark treats NaN as bigger than every other number, so `> 0` is true.

concept.prompt: A pressure column holds -9999 meaning "no reading". What does `dropna(subset=["pressure_hpa"])` do with that row?
choices: Keeps it: -9999 is an ordinary number to Spark
concept.why: Spark doesn't know the code. Replace it first with `na.replace(-9999, None, subset=[...])`, then drop or fill.

review: Find empty values with `isNull()` and `isNotNull()`; `== None` is never true.
NaN is a value, not `NULL`. Find it with `F.isnan`. In Spark NaN equals NaN and is bigger than every number.
A sentinel like -9999 is just a number to Spark. Turn it into `NULL` with `na.replace(-9999, None, subset=[...])` or `F.when`.
`dropna` drops rows with missing values; `subset`, `how` and `thresh` choose which. NaN counts as missing.
`fillna` fills missing values (and NaN in number columns); `F.coalesce` takes the first value that isn't `NULL`.
Fill only with a value that's true: a gauge fault isn't a dry hour.
